overview: Aboriginal peoples of Australia comprise many nations with their own languages, knowledge and relationships to Country. A continent-wide label cannot describe one kingdom or one way of life. The examples here come mainly from the mainland and identify particular places; Torres Strait Islander peoples have distinct histories.

periods.title: Many local histories and food systems
periods.summary: At Budj Bim, evidence of Gunditjmara aquaculture extends back at least 6,600 years. This is one long regional history within a diverse continent, not the beginning of all Aboriginal societies or a claim that every community used the same technologies.

periods.title: Colonisation, dispossession and resistance
periods.summary: Britain established a convict settlement at Sydney Cove in 1788. Expansion brought violence, displacement and disease, while people resisted in different regions. The date marks a colonial foothold, not the immediate conquest of the entire continent.

periods.title: Constitutional change and continuing peoples
periods.summary: The 1967 referendum followed years of organised campaigning. It removed discriminatory constitutional provisions concerning population counts and Commonwealth lawmaking, becoming an important achievement in an ongoing struggle for equality.

items.text: At Madjedbebe in Mirarr Country, researchers examined grinding stones from deposits spanning the Ice Age and later periods. Wear patterns and chemical residues indicate processing of seeds and other plants. Two stones from the oldest occupation phase, GS39 and GS73, carry evidence interpreted as seed grinding.

A shaped sandstone whetstone, GS79, occurs in that early phase alongside an axe and flakes removed from ground tools. Together they support the interpretation that people made and maintained sharpened stone edges. Shape alone would be weaker evidence than this combination of objects and wear.

Red pigments on some stones also indicate grinding, but the researchers rejected many stains as contamination. Surviving pigment does not identify the images once painted, and preservation favours mineral traces over many food residues. An archaeological sample is therefore not a complete picture of daily activity.

At Budj Bim in south-western Victoria, Gunditjmara builders used volcanic stone to redirect water through channels, dams and weirs. These structures helped trap and hold short-finned eels. Their operation depended on knowledge of water flow and the animals’ seasonal movement.

Kurtonitj preserves stone house sites, eel traps, channels and trees used for smoking eels. These connected traces show a landscape of food production, processing and settlement. They are specific evidence from Gunditjmara Country, not a template for every Australian environment.

Wooden boomerangs recovered at Wyrie Swamp in South Australia in 1973 were dated to about 10,000 years ago. They demonstrate ancient woodworking, while their survival cannot establish when the first boomerang was invented. Most Australian boomerangs are not the returning form familiar from popular imagery.

Boomerangs served as hunting tools, digging implements and percussion instruments, with forms adapted to different tasks. Hooked examples from north-central Australia and heavy carved examples from the Darling and Cooper river systems travelled through exchange networks. Technique and decoration varied among makers and communities.

People in colder regions made clothing from animal skins. In Noongar language, kangaroo-skin cloaks are called booka. The museum also holds a 2005 reproduction by Lee Darroch and Treahna Hamm of a possum-skin cloak collected at Echuca in 1853, linking practical clothing to cultural renewal.

Seasonal knowledge guides activities on Country. In recent collaborations, Indigenous knowledge holders and CSIRO have created calendars that communicate local environmental understanding. Ngan’gi, Walmajarri and Kunwinjku projects are distinct examples, not different versions of one national calendar.

From 1792, Pemulwuy led resistance near the Parramatta, Hawkesbury and Georges rivers. His actions and the punitive colonial response show that occupation was contested. This Sydney-region history should not be assigned automatically to distant communities with different experiences of invasion.

The 1967 campaign drew on petitions, community organising and alliances. Joe McGinness and Faith Bandler were among its leading organisers. The resulting constitutional change did not first grant voting rights: the federal franchise had already been extended in 1962.

ending.text: Colonisation brought profound losses of land, lives and self-government, but Aboriginal peoples did not disappear. Communities continue in urban, regional and remote Australia, maintaining and renewing distinct identities. A change or ending in this broad map label records the atlas’s categories, not a single surrender or the end of a people.
